title: Vesali is lovely
hookLine: he looks back at the city turning his whole body, like an elephant, and says how delightful it was (DN 16)

lines: IN HIS LAST MONTHS, ENJOYING IT.
cards: The last time you left a place you loved, did you look back? The apartment emptied out, keys on the counter. A hometown in the rearview mirror.
A hospital room. Some people can't help it; they turn around at the door. Vesali was a rich, lively city, full of shrines and gardens and a proud, independent people.

The Buddha knew it well. It was where the women had walked to ask for ordination, and where a well-known courtesan named Ambapali gave him a mango grove and a meal, beating the city's princes to the invitation.
In the last months of his life, the old texts show him in Vesali, enjoying it.

teach.b: Here's a quiet surprise. Sitting at a shrine outside the city one day, the Buddha turns to Ananda and simply names the places he loves. Delightful is Vesali, Ananda.
Delightful is this shrine, and that one, and that one, and he lists them by name. An awakened man near the end of his life, enjoying the view.
Some people imagine letting go means not caring about anything, being above it all. This moment says something else.
He's free of clinging, and he can still say, this place is beautiful. Maybe that's exactly why he can say it so simply, without needing to keep it. Then comes the leaving.
After his last alms round in Vesali, as he walks away, he stops and turns to look back at the city.
The text says he looked back with the elephant look. The commentary explains the phrase: an elephant doesn't glance over its shoulder; it turns its whole great body to look, and so did he.

teach.h: THE LAST TIME I'LL SEE IT.
teach.b: And he says to Ananda: this is the last time I will look at Vesali. That's all. No speech about impermanence, though he had taught it often.
Then he turns back and walks on. Two things held together: he loves it, and he lets it go, both completely. Nothing half-turned.
One full look at the city, then the road to the next village.

how: Pilgrims still visit Vaishali in Bihar, India, where an Ashokan pillar and stupa ruins mark places tied to the Buddha's life, and the 'elephant look' is remembered in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, read across Buddhist traditions.

o: the downcast gaze monks keep on the alms round
the elephant look: turning the whole body to look back
a royal elephant that carried the Buddha's relics

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: turning the whole body to look
gave a mango grove and a meal
heard it was his last look

s: the Buddha taught that letting go means not caring about anything
near the end he calls Vesali and its shrines delightful, by name.
he turned his whole body to look back, like an elephant
the text calls it the elephant look; the commentary explains the whole-body turn.
Ambapali beat the city's princes to invite him to a meal
and gave him her mango grove.

games.q: you're leaving a city you love for the last time, and you know it. what do you do?
o: turn your whole body and look, then walk on.
games.why: he turns fully, like an elephant, and says: this is the last time I'll look at Vesali. then he walks on.

practice: Bring to mind a place you loved and left, a childhood kitchen, a school, a city, a friend's porch, and walk through it slowly, seeing the light, hearing it.
Then, the way an elephant turns, turn your whole attention toward it and say quietly: how lovely it was. Let it be lovely, then let it be past.

wordCard.voice: Nagapalokita. The elephant look: the Buddha turning his whole body toward Vesali, the places he loved, for one last look.

orig.note: Pali: the elephant look. Naga (elephant) and apalokita (looking back).

carryVoice: Your line: how lovely it was. Free of clinging, and still able to call a place delightful. Day eighty, done.
